people.name: Jesus of Nazareth
people.short_bio: Central figure of Christianity. Jewish teacher from Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate c. AD 30; confessed by Christians as the Messiah and Son of God. Called and taught the Twelve Apostles.

people.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
people.short_bio: Mother of Jesus of Nazareth. Present at the crucifixion and entrusted to the disciple John; numbered among the disciples gathered before Pentecost.

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.short_bio: Disciple of Jesus from Magdala in Galilee; first witness of the resurrection in all four Gospels. Called 'apostle to the apostles' by later tradition.

people.name: Peter
people.short_bio: Chief of the Twelve Apostles. Fisherman from Bethsaida; preached at Pentecost, traveled widely, and traditionally martyred in Rome under Nero. Counted by Roman tradition as first bishop of Rome.

people.name: Andrew
people.short_bio: Brother of Peter, fisherman from Bethsaida, one of the Twelve. Traditionally evangelized Scythia and Achaea and was crucified at Patras.

people.name: James, son of Zebedee
people.short_bio: Brother of John, son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve and of the inner three. Beheaded by Herod Agrippa I c. AD 44 — the first apostle martyred.

people.name: John the Apostle
people.short_bio: Son of Zebedee, brother of James, one of the Twelve and of the inner three. By tradition resided in Ephesus, taught Polycarp and Papias, and lived to the reign of Trajan.

people.name: Philip the Apostle
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve, from Bethsaida. Tradition (via Polycrates of Ephesus in Eusebius) places his later life and burial at Hierapolis in Phrygia.

people.name: Bartholomew
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve, often identified with Nathanael. Tradition reports preaching in India and Armenia and martyrdom by flaying.

people.name: Matthew the Apostle
people.short_bio: Tax collector called by Jesus, one of the Twelve, traditionally the author of the Gospel of Matthew (originally in 'the Hebrew dialect' per Papias).

people.name: Thomas the Apostle
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve. Confessed the risen Christ as 'My Lord and my God' (John 20). Traditionally evangelized Parthia and India.

people.name: James, son of Alphaeus
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve, distinguished from James son of Zebedee. Often (and disputedly) identified with James the Less or James the Just.

people.name: Jude Thaddaeus
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve, called Thaddaeus in Matthew/Mark and 'Jude of James' in Luke. Traditional author of the Epistle of Jude in some attributions.

people.name: Simon the Zealot
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve, called the Zealot or Cananean. Few details survive; later traditions place his mission in Persia or Britain.

people.name: Judas Iscariot
people.short_bio: One of the Twelve who betrayed Jesus to the Sanhedrin for thirty pieces of silver. Died shortly thereafter (by hanging in Matthew; by falling in Acts).

people.name: Matthias
people.short_bio: Chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot among the Twelve (Acts 1). Tradition reports later mission to Cappadocia or Ethiopia.

people.name: Paul of Tarsus
people.short_bio: Pharisee turned apostle to the Gentiles after his Damascus-road encounter. Author of at least seven undisputed letters in the New Testament; martyred in Rome under Nero.

people.name: James the Just
people.short_bio: Brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church. Presided at the Apostolic Council (Acts 15); martyred c. 62 by stoning under high priest Ananus per Josephus and Hegesippus.

people.name: Mark the Evangelist
people.short_bio: Companion of Paul and Barnabas, then 'interpreter' of Peter at Rome (per Papias). Traditional author of the Gospel of Mark and founder of the church of Alexandria.

people.name: Luke the Evangelist
people.short_bio: Physician and companion of Paul, traditional author of the Gospel of Luke and Acts of the Apostles. Identified by Irenaeus as 'a follower of Paul'.

people.name: Timothy
people.short_bio: Companion and disciple of Paul, addressee of 1-2 Timothy. Traditionally first bishop of Ephesus; martyred under Nerva or Trajan per later acta.

people.name: Titus
people.short_bio: Greek companion of Paul, addressee of the Epistle to Titus. Left in Crete to organize the church; traditionally first bishop of Gortyna.

people.name: Onesimus
people.short_bio: Slave of Philemon converted by Paul (Philem. 10). Often identified with the bishop Onesimus of Ephesus greeted by Ignatius in his letter to the Ephesians.

people.name: Linus of Rome
people.short_bio: Listed by Irenaeus and Eusebius as the first bishop of Rome after Peter and Paul. Often identified with the Linus greeted in 2 Timothy 4:21.

people.name: Anacletus of Rome
people.short_bio: Second successor of Peter at Rome per Irenaeus' list. Almost no biographical detail survives beyond the succession lists.

people.name: Clement of Rome
people.short_bio: Bishop of Rome late in the 1st century. Author of 1 Clement to the Corinthian church c. AD 96 — the earliest surviving Christian document outside the New Testament.

people.name: Evodius of Antioch
people.short_bio: First bishop of Antioch after Peter per Eusebius and Origen. Said to have coined the term 'Christian' in some later traditions.

people.name: Ignatius of Antioch
people.short_bio: Bishop of Antioch, arrested and sent to Rome under Trajan c. 107-110, writing seven letters en route to the churches and to Polycarp. Martyred in Rome.

citations.source: Ignatius, Letters (Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, To Polycarp)

people.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
people.short_bio: Bishop of Smyrna and (per Irenaeus) disciple of John the Apostle. Wrote to the Philippians; martyred by burning c. 155-156. Teacher of Irenaeus of Lyons.

citations.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus (in Eusebius HE 5.20)

people.name: Papias of Hierapolis
people.short_bio: Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia. Author of the lost five-book 'Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord'; preserves the earliest testimony about the composition of Matthew and Mark.

people.name: Hermas
people.short_bio: Roman Christian, brother of Pope Pius I per the Muratorian Fragment. Author of 'The Shepherd of Hermas', a widely read apocalyptic-paraenetic work of the early 2nd century.

people.name: Author of the Didache
people.short_bio: Anonymous compiler of the 'Teaching of the Twelve Apostles' (Didache), an early church manual on ethics, baptism, eucharist, and ministry. Likely Syrian, late 1st or early 2nd century.

people.name: Pseudo-Barnabas
alt_names: Author of the Epistle of Barnabas
people.short_bio: Anonymous early-2nd-century author of the Epistle of Barnabas, an allegorical-typological treatise on the Old Testament. Probably Alexandrian; not in fact the apostolic Barnabas.

people.name: Quadratus of Athens
people.short_bio: Earliest known Christian apologist, who addressed an apology to Hadrian c. 124-129. Eusebius preserves a single fragment claiming some healed by Christ survived 'into our own times'.

people.name: Aristides of Athens
people.short_bio: Athenian philosopher and Christian apologist who addressed an Apology to Hadrian (or Antoninus Pius). His Apology survives in Syriac, Greek (in Barlaam and Josaphat), and Armenian.

relationships.notes: Peter is called by Jesus and named chief of the Twelve in all four Gospels.
One of the Twelve who later betrayed Jesus.
Acts 1:21-22 specifies Matthias had accompanied Jesus 'beginning from the baptism of John' though he was not one of the original Twelve.
Brother of Jesus per Mark 6:3 and Galatians 1:19; received a resurrection appearance per 1 Cor 15:7.
Paul claims a resurrection appearance and direct revelation (Galatians 1:11-17, 1 Cor 15:8). Not a pre-Easter disciple.
Paul visited Cephas in Jerusalem for fifteen days c. AD 36 (Gal 1:18). They later met at the Apostolic Council (Gal 2 / Acts 15).
The Antioch incident: Paul publicly rebuked Peter for withdrawing from Gentile table fellowship under pressure from 'men from James' (Gal 2:11-14).
Paul met James in Jerusalem (Gal 1:19) and again at the Apostolic Council (Gal 2:9 / Acts 15).

Paul was opposed not by James personally but by 'certain men from James' whose intervention triggered the Antioch incident (Gal 2:12). The direct opposition between Paul and James himself is inferred and disputed by scholars.
Luke is named as Paul's companion in Colossians 4:14, Philemon 24, 2 Timothy 4:11; Irenaeus calls him 'a follower of Paul'.
Mark accompanied Paul and Barnabas, then split (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39). Later reconciled (Col 4:10; 2 Tim 4:11).

Papias (c. 110-130) reports Mark was Peter's interpreter and recorded Peter's preaching as the Gospel of Mark — but Papias' testimony itself survives only via Eusebius. 1 Peter 5:13 mentions 'Mark my son' but does not establish discipleship.

Irenaeus, who personally heard Polycarp in his youth, states in Adv. Haer. 3.3.4 and his Letter to Florinus (Eus. HE 5.20) that Polycarp was instructed by John and 'others who had seen the Lord'. This is a near-contemporary chain (Irenaeus -> Polycarp -> John), so 'documented'.

citations.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius HE 5.20.4-8

relationships.notes: Later tradition (e.g. the Martyrium Ignatii and John Chrysostom) makes Ignatius a disciple of John alongside Polycarp; not attested by Ignatius himself or by Irenaeus.

Irenaeus calls Papias 'a hearer of John' (Adv. Haer. 5.33.4), but Eusebius (HE 3.39.5-7), reading Papias' own preface, argues Papias heard 'the elder John', a different figure. Borderline — flagged for review.
Whether or not Papias heard John the Apostle directly, his preface explicitly reports gathering sayings of John (the Lord's disciple) via the elders.
Forward edge into the next era. Irenaeus in his Letter to Florinus describes hearing Polycarp preach in his youth at Smyrna.

citations.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus in Eusebius HE 5.20.4-8

relationships.notes: Irenaeus' succession list names Linus as the man to whom 'the apostles' (Peter and Paul) committed the Roman episcopate. Episcopal succession lists for 1st-c Rome were reconstructed by Irenaeus c. 180 (Adv. Haer. 3.3); not contemporaneously attested.
Roman succession list reconstructed by Irenaeus c. 180; no contemporaneous attestation.
Roman succession list reconstructed by Irenaeus c. 180; the order Linus-Anacletus-Clement is not contemporaneously attested.
Eusebius lists Evodius as first bishop of Antioch after Peter. Peter's actual episcopal tenure at Antioch is traditional rather than narrated in scripture.
Antiochene episcopal succession is preserved only by Eusebius writing c. 320; no 1st-c Antiochene source survives to confirm.
Tertullian (De Praesc. 32) says Clement was ordained by Peter. Origen and others identify him with the Clement of Phil 4:3. No first-person testimony survives — marked tradition per the brief.
1 Clement 5 speaks vividly of Paul's martyrdom in the first person plural ('our generation'); patristic tradition (Origen, Eusebius, Jerome) identifies Clement with the fellow worker of Phil 4:3.
Cross-reference target is a church not a person; included per brief. 1 Clement is addressed from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth c. AD 96 to settle a leadership dispute.
Ignatius wrote a personal letter to Polycarp en route to Rome; Polycarp in turn forwarded the corpus of Ignatian letters to the Philippians (Phil 13).
Ignatius greets a Bishop Onesimus of Ephesus in his Letter to the Ephesians; the identification with Paul's freed slave Onesimus is traditional and not certain.
Irenaeus (Adv. Haer. 5.33.4) calls Papias 'a companion of Polycarp'. No surviving first-person source.
Strictly an apostolic succession (not episcopal) — Matthias chosen by lot to replace Judas among the Twelve.
Roman Catholic tradition treats Peter as Christ's vicar / successor in pastoral leadership of the Church (Matt 16:18-19); not framed as episcopal succession in the New Testament itself.
Papias preserves the earliest tradition about Mark's authorship and method.
Quadratus' surviving fragment claims firsthand testimony was still alive in his day from those healed or raised by Jesus.

citations.source: Quadratus, Apology fragment in Eusebius HE 4.3.2

relationships.notes: The Shepherd (Vis. 2.4.3) instructs Hermas to give a copy of the book to 'Clement', who will send it abroad. The identification with Clement of Rome is plausible but traditional, and the Muratorian Fragment dates Hermas under Pius I (mid-2nd c.) which would post-date Clement.
Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians quotes or alludes to most of the Pauline corpus extensively.
Ignatius alludes repeatedly to Pauline letters (esp. 1 Cor, Eph) and explicitly praises Paul (Eph. 12.2; Rom. 4.3).
The Didache cites the Lord's Prayer and dominical sayings 'as the Lord commanded in his Gospel'.
Mary is the mother of Jesus per the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke; present at the wedding at Cana, the crucifixion, and with the disciples before Pentecost.
From the cross Jesus entrusted his mother to the Beloved Disciple, who took her into his own home (John 19:26-27).

Clement of Alexandria quotes the Epistle of Barnabas as scripture in the Stromata, attributing it to the apostolic Barnabas. Marked tradition because Pseudo-Barnabas himself is anonymous; Clement is citing the text under a pseudepigraphic attribution.
Origen quotes the Epistle of Barnabas as a 'catholic epistle' (Contra Celsum 1.63). Marked tradition because Pseudo-Barnabas is anonymous and Origen attributes the text to the apostolic Barnabas.
Eusebius discusses the Epistle of Barnabas among the disputed/spurious writings (HE 3.25, 6.14). Marked tradition because the author is anonymous.
